title: Balochistan 'Declares Independence' From Pakistan, Seeks Indian Embassy in Delhi
excerpt: Self-proclaimed Baloch leader Mir Yar Baloch claims control over 85 percent of the province and calls for UN recognition, but no country has acknowledged the declaration.
body:
• Baloch activist Mir Yar Baloch declared the formation of the 'Republic of Balochistan' on July 15, claiming 85 percent territorial control.
  • The declaration includes a national flag, anthem, and a new currency called the Balochi Falus — none recognized by any country.
  • Baloch leadership has called on India to open a Baloch embassy in New Delhi and urged the UN to deploy peacekeeping forces.
  • Pakistan has not officially responded, and no government or international body has recognized the claim.

A Declaration Without Recognition

A self-declared Baloch leadership announced the formation of an independent Republic of Balochistan on July 15, claiming control over most of Pakistan's largest province and appealing to the international community for diplomatic recognition. The announcement was made by Mir Yar Baloch, who describes himself as a representative of the Baloch independence movement, through a series of posts on social media platform X.

In the declaration, Mir Yar Baloch claimed that Balochistan's defense forces had secured roughly 85 percent of the province's territory and that a transitional government was being formed with guaranteed representation for Baloch women. The statement said a force of 500,000 personnel was prepared to remove Pakistani military forces from the region by the end of 2026.

"The patriotic people of the Republic of Balochistan have rejected Pakistan's external presence. Balochistan is not Pakistan."

— Mir Yar Baloch, Baloch Independence Activist

"Balochistan is not Pakistan."</p><cite>— Mir Yar Baloch, Baloch Independence Activist</cite></blockquote> <p>None of these claims have been independently verified."

None of these claims have been independently verified. Pakistan has not officially acknowledged the declaration, and no country or international organization has extended recognition.

What the Declaration Claims

According to the statement, the self-proclaimed republic has adopted a national anthem titled 'Ma Chukain Balochani,' introduced a national flag, and announced its own currency, the Balochi Falus. The declaration also asserted control over key natural resources including gas fields, coal mines, and major deposits of gold and copper that make Balochistan one of the most mineral-rich regions in South Asia.

The leadership further claimed that thousands of personnel from Pakistan's military and security agencies had defected to the Baloch cause, though this remains unverified by any independent source.

Why This Matters for India

In a pointed appeal to New Delhi, Mir Yar Baloch called on the Indian government to allow the opening of a Baloch embassy in the capital. He extended what he described as full support for India's position on Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, urging the international community to press Pakistan to vacate the region.

The overture to India is not new. Baloch separatist leaders have periodically sought Indian backing, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi referenced Balochistan in an Independence Day speech in 2016, drawing sharp protests from Islamabad. For New Delhi, the declaration presents a delicate diplomatic situation — any overt engagement could escalate tensions with Pakistan, while ignoring it risks losing leverage in the broader geopolitical contest over South Asian influence.

Decades of Conflict

Balochistan has been the site of a long-running separatist insurgency since Pakistan's annexation of the former Kalat State in 1948. The region, which borders Iran and Afghanistan and sits along critical trade routes including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, has seen repeated military crackdowns, enforced disappearances, and armed resistance over seven decades.

The Balochistan Liberation Army and other armed groups have carried out attacks on Pakistani military targets, Chinese-funded infrastructure projects, and government installations. Pakistan has consistently labeled the movement as terrorism backed by foreign powers, while human rights organizations have documented widespread abuses against Baloch civilians.

What's Next

Without international recognition, the declaration remains a symbolic political claim rather than a shift in territorial reality. Pakistan's military retains operational control over the province, and major powers including the United States, China, and the European Union have not commented on the announcement. The Baloch movement's ability to sustain momentum will depend on whether it can secure any form of diplomatic engagement beyond social media declarations.

For the Indian diaspora, the development is worth watching as a barometer of India-Pakistan tensions. Any Indian government response — or deliberate silence — will signal broader strategic calculations in the region.
